newsitem.title: CANADA: Popular support for Quebec separatists slumps.
newsitem.headline: Popular support for Quebec separatists slumps.

text.p: Canada's French-speaking province of Quebec appeared headed for a long winter as public displeasure with budget cuts and economic woes has dampened the popularity of its separatist government.

A poll published on Thursday in the Globe and Mail newspaper showed growing dissatisfaction with the Parti Quebecois government, led by Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard. The survey found 56 percent of the 1,005 voters questioned were not satisfied with the government -- a jump from its 49 percent disapproval rating in a similar poll just a month ago.
"The results show the effects of the government's cutbacks," Jean-Marc Leger, president of polling firm Groupe Leger & Leger, told the newspaper.

In an effort to meet his forecast of a steadily declining budget defict -- to C$2.2 billion (US$1.6 billion) by March 31, 1998, from a forecast C$3.2 (US$2.4 billion) billion this spring -- Bouchard was seeking government spending cuts of at least C$2.6 billion (US$1.9 billion).

The reductions in funding for hospitals and other health services, education and salaries for Quebec's 440,000 public employees come as the province is locked in a desperate struggle with a 12.6 percent unemployment rate and 800,000 of its 7.1 million residents living on government welfare.

The budget cuts have drawn a backlash from the province's poor, unemployed, students and women's groups. Big public sector unions, traditional allies of Quebec's sovereignty movement, were also protesting the cuts that spare no one.
"Everyone will be asked to participate in this effort," Bouchard said at a press conference on Thursday.

But his plan to clean up Quebec's fiscal problems and put it on strong footing before seeking separation and some form of economic or political "partnership" with the rest of Canada, has sowed dissent among his separatist allies.

On Thursday local newspapers published an open letter by Jacques Parizeau, who relinquished his premiership and leadership of the Parti Quebecois to the more popular Bouchard in January, blasting his successor's strategies and saying separation must come regardless of any offers of partnership.

"Sovereignty is dropping in the polls. Federalists attack it incessantly. The counterattack is rare and weak. You don't 'sell' sovereignty by hiding it," Parizeau wrote in the Globe and Mail and Quebec City's Le Soleil.

The separatists' sagging political fortunes are seen in the contest for a new leader of the Bloc Quebecois, a separatist party that won the majority of Quebec seats in Canada's 1993 national parliamentary elections.

Without a charismatic leader like Bouchard, who left the Bloc to become Quebec premier, the party was in jeopardy of faltering in a federal election expected next year and of losing its status as the official opposition in Ottawa.

A 1997 election would be the fifth time in six years that the vote-weary Quebec electorate has cast ballots in elections or referenda. In October 1995, Quebec separatists lost a referendum vote on sovereignty by about one percentage point.

The poll published on Thursday showed federalists maintaining a slim lead of 52 percent to 48 percent over sovereignists on the question of whether Quebec should secede. Political analysts say the worst may be ahead for the 58-year-old Bouchard and his separatist allies.
